same class of error as overstating one — it is a claim that does not match the
evidence, and the direction of the mismatch does not make it honest. The title
now reads "makes it worse". The abstract also carries the `size` replication,
which landed in the previous entry and had not reached the front.

**The abstract's one piece of comfort had never been measured.** It says three
seeds "are enough to get the sign of an effect right and nowhere near enough to
get its size right". That sentence predates any arm going to eight seeds. It is
the only reassuring thing this paper says about small budgets, and everything
around it — sizes wrong, existence wrong in both directions, nulls that are not
nulls — is measured. Leaving the reassurance as the single unmeasured claim in
the paragraph is precisely the asymmetry a reader should not have to catch.

Checkable, because twelve arms now have both a three-seed measurement (seeds
0-2) and an eight-seed one on the same cells:

**0 of 12 changed sign.** The three-seed estimate of the magnitude ranged from
0.62 to 2.15 times the eight-seed one — so it is wrong by up to a factor of two
in either direction while never pointing the wrong way. The sentence survives,
and now with numbers behind it.

One caveat I put in the JSON rather than the abstract: the three-seed set is a
*subset* of the eight-seed set, not an independent replication. This measures
what an experimenter who stopped early would have concluded, which is the
practically relevant question, but it is not evidence that three fresh seeds
would agree — they share three of their draws by construction. A cleaner test
would compare disjoint triples, and that is not something these runs support.

The pattern across entries 74, 80 and this one is the same: the documents drift
from the evidence in small ways that no guard catches, because every guard here
asks whether a number is current and none asks whether a *sentence* still
matches what was found. Re-reading the front matter against the run outputs
found three such gaps in three sittings, which is a high enough hit rate that it
should be a standing item rather than something I do when a turn is otherwise
free.

### 87. H70 confirmed, every null is powered, and success deleted the section that said so

`focal_complete.sh` finished. All five gammas at eight seeds against the
bit-exact γ = 0 control:

| γ | vs γ = 0 | p | floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | +0.00298 | 0.4880 | 0.00016 |
| 1.0 | +0.00248 | 0.5722 | 0.00016 |
| 2.0 | -0.00032 | 0.9442 | 0.00016 |
| 5.0 | -0.00288 | 0.5573 | 0.00016 |

**H70 confirmed: none separates.** And with it, **7 of 7 comparisons across all
three null families can now return p < 0.05**, against two of seven when the
power audit was first written. Every null this project rests on is a null a test
could have rejected — which is the difference between reporting that we found
nothing and reporting that there is nothing to find. "Focal loss contributes
nothing" is now a measurement rather than a shrug, which matters because the
target that started this work named focal loss as though it were the mechanism.

**Then the failure of the turn, and it is a good one.** Section 7.9 — the
section documenting exactly this — was guarded by
`if npa and npa.get("n_underpowered")`. The moment the last underpowered null
was fixed, `n_underpowered` became 0 and **the entire section silently
disappeared from the paper**, taking with it the evidence that the problem had
been solved.

A section conditioned on the presence of a defect deletes the record of the
defect being fixed. That is a design error and not a typo, and it is the kind
that only fires on success — which means it would never have appeared in any
amount of testing against a broken repository.

**No guard caught it, and I can say precisely why.** `section_census.py` asks
whether every input a generator reads is present: `null_power_audit.json` was
present. `coverage_check.py` asks whether every run family is referenced by some
generator: it is, in the source. `prose_status_lint.py` asks about duplicated
paragraphs and stale status words. All six checks passed on a paper that had
just lost a section. Every guard here reasons about *inputs and source*; none
compares the rendered document against what it contained last time.

I noticed only because `_allp`, a variable I had just added inside that section,
did not raise a `NameError` — code that should have crashed ran cleanly, which
is only possible if it never executed. Being saved by an accident of my own
half-finished patch is not a process.

The obvious guard is a document-shape diff: warn when a regeneration removes a
heading that the previous version had. That is a real gap and I am recording it
as one rather than building it in the last minutes of the weekend, because a
guard written in a hurry is how `number_provenance` ended up vacuous and how the
first `section_census` passed its own broken repo. It belongs on the list for
whoever picks this up, with the failure that motivates it written down.

The guard is now `if npa and npa.get("families")` — conditioned on the data
existing rather than on the problem existing.

### 88. The guard for entry 87, built with time rather than in a hurry

Entry 87 named a gap and deliberately did not fill it: every check here reasons
about inputs and generator source, none compares the rendered document against
what it contained last time, and section 7.9 of the paper vanished without a
single check noticing. I recorded it rather than building it in the last minutes
of the weekend, on the grounds that a guard written in a hurry is how
`number_provenance`'s traceability half ended up accepting 86% of random numbers
and how the first `section_census` passed its own broken repository.

`section_diff.py` snapshots each document's headings and fails when one is
removed. Added headings are reported and never fail — documents are meant to
grow — and a deliberate removal is recorded with `--accept`, which leaves a diff
in git rather than silence.

**Two things went right that would not have gone right in a hurry.**

*The test failed first, and it was the test that was wrong.* My first assertion
looked for the literal "7.9" in the removed heading; the guard reported
`# How much each null could have shown`. The guard had caught the removal
correctly — I had written an assertion against my own implementation rather than
against the behaviour.

*And that failure exposed a real design flaw.* I had normalised every number in
a heading to `#`, so that a title carrying a measured value would not read as
removed when the value moved. That also erased section *numbering*, making
`## 7.9 Foo` and `## 8.1 Foo` the same heading — so the guard would have been
blind to renumbering, which is exactly the sort of silent restructuring it
exists to surface. Checking the actual documents, no heading carries a measured
value at all, so the normalisation is now narrow: a decimal with three or more
fraction digits, or a percentage. The test asserts both directions — a moving
p-value in a title must not look like a removal, and a renumbered section must.

That flaw was reachable only because the first version was tested against
something other than its own construction. A guard tested only on the example
that motivated it inherits whatever the author already believed.

It is in `check_all.py` (7 checks) and in `guard_audit.py` (10 of 11 now
demonstrably reject a defect they claim to catch), fed the same defect that
produced it: a section conditioned on a problem that has since been fixed.

**Meanwhile, the last hypothesis in the paper without a powered test is
running.** `paper_draft.md` has said all weekend that on `lot_time` the RPCA
residual leads both controls at every seed and that this is recorded as a
hypothesis, not a result. At three seeds the lead is about 0.013 — smaller than
`lot_time`'s own floor of 0.0187, so inside the spread of re-running one
configuration unchanged.

**H72, on record:** the residual does not separate from the zeros channel on
`lot_time` either. The argument is structural and is the one that predicted the
tight `lot` null correctly — `stack_channels` concatenates the fourth channel to
an intact one-hot, so the encoder reads an untouched copy of whatever was
removed, and that is a property of the input pipeline which does not know which
protocol it is under. What would make me wrong: leading at 3 of 3 seeds happens
by chance a quarter of the time but is not nothing, and `lot_time` orders lots in
production time, so a tool signature is likelier to carry information there than
anywhere else. If it survives eight seeds, section 4.1 needs rewriting rather
than extending.

Fresh arms under the `lot` ablation's tags rather than topping up the existing
three, because those carry tags from an earlier session and this project has
already been bitten once by mixing seeds measured in different sessions on
different GPUs.

### 89. The five-minute version had drifted to 5.4, and the fix is a budget rather than a trim

Entry 74 found `WEEKEND.md` at 5,184 words — twenty-two minutes against a brief
asking for five — and split it into a core above a stop marker and a body below,
with the core measured into the text at 949 words.

Measuring it once does not keep it measured. Since that split the core has taken
a clause per turn: the sinkhorn verdict, the `size` replication, the RPCA tie at
118 times below the floor. Each addition was locally right — every one of them
is a real result and belongs in a summary of the weekend. Together they carried
the core to **1,237 words, 5.4 minutes**, which is the original failure running
slower.

The document was not lying about it. It reports its own reading time, and 5.4
rounds to "about 5 minutes", so the drift was visible to anyone who divided.
That is exactly the kind of true-but-unread number this project keeps finding.

**So the fix is a check, not a trim.** `reading_budget.py` fails when the core
exceeds five minutes at 230 words per minute — the five comes from the brief and
the rate is stated in the script so it can be argued with rather than assumed.
It is in `check_all.py` (8 checks) and `guard_audit.py` (11 of 12), fed a core
that has drifted and one that has not.

Trimming to pass it was the smaller half of the work and worth recording for
what it revealed about how the drift happens. Nothing was deleted; four bullets
were carrying explanations that the detail sections already give in full:

  * the RPCA bullet re-derived why the control could not have differed;
  * the sinkhorn bullet reproduced most of §2.3a's diagnosis;
  * the DG bullet printed `p = 0.00781` three times in four sentences;
  * the "what needs a human" paragraph restated all four decisions that
    section 4 sets out with options, when only one of them actually blocks
    work — the metrology cost model, which nobody in this repository can settle.

The pattern is that a summary bullet drifts toward becoming the section it
summarises, because each turn the most recent finding feels like the one that
needs explaining. Naming the *claim* and pointing at the section is the job; the
mechanism is what the pointer is for.

**A note on what this check cannot do.** It counts words. A core could pass at
1,148 words and still be unreadable, or could pass by cutting a finding rather
than moving detail below the marker — the script says so in its own failure
message, which is the only defence available. It enforces a budget, not quality,
and the distinction matters because the previous entry's guard has the same
shape: `section_diff.py` notices a heading vanishing and cannot notice a section
becoming wrong.

### 90. The README described a benchmark this repository does not contain

Nine documents' worth of checks, and none of them looks at `README.md` — it is
the only document here that is not generated, so nothing regenerates it when the
code grows and no guard notices when it stops being true. It is also the first
thing anyone picking this up reads.

Reading it against `run_bench.py` and `wts/methods.py`:

| the README said | the code has |
|---|---|
| "The three protocols", three-row table | **four** — `lot_time` missing entirely |
| "Four representations", three-row table | **six** — `graph` and `rpca_cnn` missing |
| "Seven objectives" | **eleven** |

None of these is a typo. Each is a place where the code grew and the prose
introducing it did not, and the omissions are not random: the missing protocol
is `lot_time`, which carries the largest drop in the project, and one of the
missing representations is `rpca_cnn` — this repository's own contribution, the
one whose withdrawal the README's closing section is *about*. A reader would
have formed a wrong picture of the benchmark's scope before reaching a number.

The same section also still said the RPCA channel and a channel of zeros "are
indistinguishable at three seeds", which was the honest statement when written
and has been superseded twice over: at eight seeds they are 0.000046 apart, 118
times below the floor, with a test that could have resolved a difference 35
times smaller than the floor. Three seeds could not have contradicted the
withdrawal whatever the truth was, which is why it was re-run, and the README now
says both things.

**`readme_sync.py` checks the counts the README states against the ones the code
defines.** It cannot check that the *descriptions* are right — that still needs
reading — but a count is exactly the part that drifts silently while every
sentence around it stays plausible.

**Its first run reported a mismatch that was the checker's fault.** It said the
README claimed eleven objectives and the code had seven. `OBJECTIVES` is built
from a dict literal and then extended by an `.update()` three hundred lines
later; my parser read the literal and stopped. Had I trusted it I would have
"corrected" a right README to a wrong number, which is a worse outcome than the
drift it was built to catch. The audit now cross-checks the parser against
`len(methods.OBJECTIVES)` by importing, so the two disagreeing is itself a
failure.

That makes twice in this session that a summary missed a member added elsewhere
— the power audit collapsing a family to its weakest comparison, and this parser
reading the first of two definitions. Both were caught by comparing against an
independent count rather than by reading the code more carefully.

`check_all.py` is now nine checks; `guard_audit.py` twelve of thirteen.

### 91. H72: the last hypothesis in the paper, and the pattern behind it was a coin

`paper_draft.md` has said all weekend that on `lot_time` the RPCA residual leads
both controls at every seed, that this is the one protocol where a genuine tool
signature should help, and that it is recorded as a hypothesis rather than a
result. It was the last claim in the paper without a powered test.

Re-run as fresh arms at eight seeds in a single session:

| arm | n | mean | seed range |
|---|---|---|---|
| residual | 8 | 0.7074 | 0.0252 |
| failmask | 8 | 0.7065 | 0.0358 |
| zeros | 8 | 0.7045 | 0.0221 |

Residual against a channel of zeros: **+0.00288, p = 0.4656**, floor 0.00016 —
seven times below `lot_time`'s own run-to-run floor of 0.0187. **H72 confirmed:
it does not help there either.**

**And the observation that made it worth testing dissolved.** "Ahead at every
seed" was three of three, which a coin gives a quarter of the time. At eight
seeds the residual leads on **five of eight**, which is what a coin does. The
three-seed effect of about 0.013 shrank to 0.00288.

That is the fourth time this weekend a three-seed pattern has evaporated, and
the first where the pattern was a *sign count* rather than a magnitude. Worth
separating: entry 86 established that three seeds get the sign of an aggregate
effect right in 12 of 12 arms, and that remains true. What three seeds cannot do
is make "led at every seed" mean anything, because three coin flips agree a
quarter of the time. Both statements are about small samples and they are not in
tension; one is about the sign of a mean, the other about the frequency of a
streak.

The structural argument now holds on both protocols where it was tested:
`stack_channels` concatenates the fourth channel to an intact one-hot, so the
encoder always holds an untouched copy of whatever the decomposition removed —
a property of the input pipeline, which does not know which protocol it is
under. On `lot` the arms tie to 0.000046; on `lot_time` to 0.00288. Every claim
in the paper is now either measured with a test that could have rejected it, or
marked `[not measured]`.

**The reading-budget check from entry 89 fired on its first turn in service.**
Adding "on both protocols where it was tested" to a core bullet put
`WEEKEND.md` six words over five minutes. Its failure message says the fix is to
move detail below the marker rather than delete a finding, so that is what
happened: the core bullet went back to its earlier wording and the `lot_time`
result went into §2.1 in full. A guard whose advice is followed on the first
occasion is a better sign than one that passes.

**Two process notes, both mine.** The insertion first landed at the wrong
indentation and broke `weekend.py`, which the regeneration reported immediately;
I then tried to repair the indentation in place and made it worse, mixing
twelve- and sixteen-space levels in one block. Reverting the file and redoing
the edit against a verified line number took less time than the second repair
attempt. And `critique_log.md` reached 91 entries and 43,000 words with no
index, so one is now generated by `scripts/critique_index.py` and checked by
`check_all.py` — hand-maintaining it would be the defect entry 90 found in the
README.

### 92. Nine checks passed on a document its generator could no longer produce

The pooling result is the only thing in this project that worked, and section
2.0 has ended all weekend with "It is still one encoder." That caveat is honest
and had never been tested: every `poolmean` / `poolmeanmax` / `poolmeanmean`
cell here is `cnn_gn`.

`cnn_bn` differs in the normalisation layer alone — same three blocks, same
width, same head, the same 290,217 parameters under `meanmax` — so repeating
the comparison there isolates the interaction between pooling and normalisation
and nothing else. Twenty-four cells are running.

**H73, before the run:** the `Scratch` gain replicates. `meanmax` beats `mean`
at p < 0.05 with eight seeds per arm, and `meanmean` does not. The mechanism is
about what global average pooling *discards* — a thin connected line averaged
over a wafer is close to a slightly elevated background failure rate — which is
a fact about the class and the operator, not about a normalisation layer.

**Why it might fail, written down before the data:** BatchNorm mixes statistics
across whatever is in the batch, which this project already found to be a domain
leak when batches span lots. Max pooling passes extreme activations through, and
under BN one wafer's extreme shifts the normalisation of the others — so the
statistic `meanmax` adds is precisely the kind BN is least able to keep
separate. Both outcomes are worth having: replication makes this architectural,
failure makes it a GroupNorm result and the section should say so in its title.
The generator is already wired to write whichever way it lands.

**And the turn produced a better finding than the experiment will.** My patch to
`paper.py` had the wrong indentation and raised before writing. I then ran
`check_all.py` and **all ten checks passed** — on the previous
`paper_draft.md`, which was still sitting on disk. Its inputs were present, its
runs were referenced, nothing was duplicated, no number had been typed, no
heading had vanished, the core was under budget. Every one of those was true,
and every one was about a document the generator could no longer produce.

The structural error is that **every check here reads a file, and a file on disk
is the last *successful* output.** A crashed generator is therefore invisible to
all of them simultaneously, and the more checks I added the more reassuring the
silence became. This is the third time this session a patch has died before
writing while surrounding commands printed successes; the first two were caught
by grepping the rendered document for the new sentence, and this one only
because the `IndentationError` happened to print directly above a `PASS`.

`generators_run.py` runs each generator to a temporary path and requires a zero
exit and a non-empty file. It is the cheapest check in the repository and it
runs first, because it is the one that decides whether the other ten are about
anything. `check_all.py` is eleven checks; `guard_audit.py` thirteen of
fourteen.

Worth stating plainly: I have now added six guards this session, and the one
that mattered most was for a failure mode created *by* having many guards — the
comfort of a long green list. A check that reads an artefact cannot tell you the
artefact is stale, and no number of such checks adds up to one that can.

### 93. 625 cells, twelve versions of the runner, and no cell says which

Entry 92 ended on a sentence worth following up: a check that reads an artefact
cannot tell you the artefact is stale. That applies to the run JSONs as much as
to the documents.

`scripts/run_bench.py` changed **thirteen times** over the weekend — new flags,
the `invariance_domain` refactor, `geometry_decomposition`, a batch dict that
gained `hw`. Dating every run file against that commit history, the **625 stored
cells span twelve distinct states of the runner**, and **none of them records
which one wrote it**.

Two of those changes were asserted bit-identical on the default path and the
rest were additive. That is the intent, and I believe it. But intent is what the
assertion covers, and the assertion was made once at the time of the change,
against the code — not against the cells. There is no way to look at a given
JSON and know which version produced it, so a table comparing a Friday cell to a
Monday cell has no way to establish that they were measured by the same
instrument.

**This is the same class of gap this project has already measured, one level
up.** Seed spread understates total variability because seeds run back to back;
the Friday cells measured on GPUs 2 and 3 sit *outside* the range of six repeats
of the same configuration; and the paper says both. A code version is a stronger
version of "which session, which device", and it is the one form of provenance
that was never recorded at all.

I want to be careful about what this does and does not say. The measurement is
file mtime against commit time, which is an upper bound on exposure: a commit
may change nothing a given cell uses, and most of these did not. It is not a
claim that any number here is wrong, and I have not found one that is. It is a
claim that the question is currently unanswerable per cell, which is a
different and smaller thing — and exactly the kind of smaller thing this project
has spent the weekend learning to state rather than assume away.

It is now threat 5 in the paper, with the counts generated from
`runs/run_provenance.json`.

**The fix is two fields and is queued rather than applied.** `git_sha` and
`written_at` cannot affect any measurement, so there was a real temptation to
patch `run_bench.py` immediately. A sweep is in flight. Editing the runner
mid-sweep would leave half its cells labelled and half not — an inhomogeneity
introduced by the act of recording provenance, which would be a poor joke and a
real confound. `scripts/add_run_provenance.sh` waits for the lease and then
patches, which is the same discipline as `chain3.sh` and the reason
`chain_after_size.sh` had to be reverted: **the fact that a change is safe for
the numbers does not make it safe for the experiment.**

**Postscript to 93: both guards fired on this commit, and both were partly
wrong about themselves.**

`reading_budget.py` failed with **"OVER by 1 words"** — but it originally
printed **"OVER by 0 words"**. At 1,151 words the core is 5.0043 minutes, and
`int((5.0043 - 5) * 230)` rounds the overage to zero, so the check failed while
reporting no overage. An off-by-one in a guard's *message* costs it its
authority faster than a wrong threshold would: a reader who sees "OVER by 0"
concludes the check is broken and passes `--strict` off. Now ceil, minimum one.

`section_diff.py` reported a section REMOVED that had merely been renamed:
`RESULTS.md` titles one section after whichever cell is currently best on `lot`,
and that changed as the `cnn_bn` pooling cells landed. Technically a heading
disappeared; practically it is ordinary churn, and a guard that cries wolf on
ordinary regeneration teaches its reader to `--accept` without looking, which is
how a check stops being a check. It now distinguishes a rename — a removed and
an added heading at the same level sharing a long prefix — from a removal, and
reports renames without failing.

**The line between the two cases matters and I nearly drew it in the wrong
place.** My first instinct was to absorb *renumbering* into "rename" as well,
and I wrote a test asserting that. Entry 88 had deliberately gone the other way:
the first version of this guard stripped every digit from a heading, which made
`7.9 Foo` and `8.1 Foo` identical and blinded it to renumbering, and narrowing
the normalisation was the fix. Absorbing renumbering into "rename" would have
undone that by a different route. A number at the front means the headings share
no prefix, so renumbering still reports as a removal and still fails; only a
change at the *tail*, where data-derived labels live, is treated as benign. The
test now says so with the reasoning attached, because I have now talked myself
out of this twice and will not remember the third time.

### 94. H73: the one positive result replicates on a second encoder

Section 2.0 has ended all weekend with "It is still one encoder." Every
`poolmean` / `poolmeanmax` / `poolmeanmean` cell in this repository was
`cnn_gn`, and that caveat had never been tested. It mattered more than a
robustness check usually would, because this is the only thing in the project
that worked — everything else was withdrawn, and a result holding on one of two
nearly identical encoders is a different claim from one holding on the
architecture.

`cnn_bn` differs in the normalisation layer alone: same three blocks, same
width, same head, the same 290,217 parameters under `meanmax`.

| comparison on `cnn_bn`, n=8 per arm | difference | exact p |
|---|---|---|
| `meanmax` vs `mean`, `Scratch` | +0.0322 | **0.01010** |
| `meanmax` vs `mean`, macro-F1 | +0.0257 | **0.00016** |
| `meanmean` vs `mean`, `Scratch` (capacity control) | +0.0130 | 0.25781 |
| `meanmean` vs `mean`, macro-F1 (capacity control) | +0.0023 | 0.61072 |

**H73 confirmed.** The treatment separates on both metrics, the capacity control
separates on neither, and the pattern matches `cnn_gn` closely enough that the
gain is not a property of GroupNorm.

**The named failure mode did not materialise, and that is worth more than the
confirmation.** Before the run I wrote down a specific reason it could fail:
BatchNorm mixes statistics across whatever is in the batch — something this
project separately established is a domain leak when batches span lots — max
pooling passes extreme activations through, and under BN one wafer's extreme
shifts the normalisation of the others, so `meanmax` adds exactly the statistic
BN is least able to keep separate. That was a real mechanism with a real
prediction, and it is wrong. If I had only written down the reason to expect
success, the confirmation would have been much weaker evidence, because a
hypothesis with no stated way to fail cannot be surprised.

Two smaller observations. macro-F1 is *more* strongly separated on `cnn_bn`
(p = 0.00016) than on `cnn_gn` (p = 0.01197), while the `Scratch` effect is
smaller (+0.0322 against +0.0473) — so the gain is spread a little more evenly
across classes here, which nothing predicted and which I am not going to explain
after the fact. And this is the first hypothesis of the weekend where the
generator was wired to write *either* outcome before the data existed; the
alternative branch is still in `paper.py` and would have said the result is a
GroupNorm finding and belongs in the section title.

The claim is now: on a lot-disjoint split, mean-and-max moves the hardest class
by 0.057 on `cnn_gn` and 0.0322 on `cnn_bn` while the capacity control moves it
by −0.001 and +0.0130 respectively, on neither encoder significantly. It remains
protocol-dependent — established on `iid`, `lot` and `lot_time`, negative on
`size` — and that dependence is measured, with no model, to be an artefact of
the resize.

**Also:** `add_run_provenance.sh` waited for the lease and patched the runner.
Every cell written from now on records `git_sha` and `written_at`. The 625
existing cells still do not, and threat 5 says so.

### 95. H74: the test that could cost the mechanism

H73 established that the pooling gain replicates on `cnn_bn`, so it is not a
GroupNorm artefact. That is a useful robustness result and a weak test of the
*explanation*, because it only asks whether the thing that works keeps working.

The stronger test is whether the thing that **fails** keeps failing, and it is
stronger because the explanation is specific about why. `resize_nearest`
upsamples by indexing, so a one-die scratch arrives as a band roughly 64/w
pixels wide — a width set by native geometry. Measured with no model: geometry
explains 0.7689 of the variance in a max-pooled line-filter response against
0.1485 of the mean-pooled one, collapsing to 0.0629 at native resolution. **That
is a property of the input pipeline, which does not know which normalisation
layer follows it.** So the `size` failure must replicate on `cnn_bn`.

**H74, before the run:** on `size` with `cnn_bn`, `meanmax` does not beat `mean`
on `Scratch` — the point estimate is at or below zero, or if positive does not
reach p < 0.05.

The phrasing is deliberately about a sign and a non-result rather than a
significant reversal, because that is what `cnn_gn` shows: -0.0427 at
p = 0.20233 on `Scratch`, negative and unestablished. Predicting a "significant
failure" would have been predicting something the reference arm does not itself
display.

**What falsification costs here is the point of running it.** If `meanmax`
significantly beats `mean` on `size`/`cnn_bn` while losing on `size`/`cnn_gn`,
the geometry explanation is wrong: the failure would be a fact about GroupNorm
rather than about the resize. Section 2.0's mechanism survived a native-
resolution control that could have killed it, and it would not survive this. I
would keep the model-free measurement — the resize really does couple apparent
width to geometry — and withdraw its connection to the `size` result, which is a
narrower and much less satisfying claim. Both branches are already written in
`paper.py`, before the data exists, as with H73.

Also topping up `cnn_gn`/`size`/`poolmeanmean` from three seeds to eight. It is
the last arm in the pooling story still at three, and a three-seed capacity
control cannot support the comparison an eight-seed treatment is making — the
exact asymmetry entry 76 found in the RPCA and focal nulls.

**The ratchet fired again**, on two numbers I typed into the new branch: the
`cnn_gn` reference effect and its p-value, both of which already sit in
`pooling_size_perm_class_Scratch.json`. That is the fifth time this session, and
the pattern is consistent enough to name: the numbers I hand-type are almost
never new measurements, they are values I have just read off a terminal while
writing prose *about* those values. The guard catches them all, which is the
only reason the rate is knowable.

### 96. The thesis, counted rather than argued

This project's central claim has been argued case by case for ninety-five
entries: results that shrank at eight seeds, a null that became two significant
effects, a streak of three-of-three that was a coin. It had never been counted.
Every comparison that reached eight seeds per arm can be re-scored on its first
three, which is exactly what an experimenter who stopped early would have had.

| | count |
|---|---|
| comparisons with eight seeds on both arms | 48 |
| of those, established at p < 0.05 with eight seeds | 17 |
| **of those, reachable with three seeds** | **0** |
| comparisons whose range-screen verdict differs at three | 8 |

**Zero of seventeen, and not through bad luck.** An exact permutation test at
three per arm admits twenty arrangements, so its smallest attainable two-sided p
is 0.10. It cannot return a value below 0.05 at any effect size whatsoever. A
three-seed protocol does not under-detect these effects — it is arithmetically
incapable of detecting any of them. Every one of the seventeen includes the
pooling result, the GroupNorm result, and both domain-generalization objectives
that turned out significantly worse than ERM.

**The range screen fails in the opposite direction, and only in that
direction.** All eight verdict changes call an effect *separated* at three seeds
and *overlapping* at eight, because a sample's range grows with the sample. The
screen gets stricter as evidence accumulates, which is the reverse of what a
reader expects and the reason this repository treats it as a floor rather than a
verdict. Stating that has been easy; showing it happens eight times out of
forty-eight and never once in the other direction is different.

**And the sharpest case is this project's own best result.** On `lot`/`cnn_bn`,
`Scratch` F1, at three seeds the range screen calls the treatment separated with
a margin of 0.0189 — and calls the **capacity control** separated with a margin
of 0.0171. At eight seeds the treatment is real (p = 0.0101) and the control is
not (p = 0.2578).

So a three-seed version of this experiment could not have distinguished *max
pooling helps* from *a wider head helps*, which is the entire question
`meanmean` exists to answer. The control would not have failed visibly. **It
would have appeared to succeed**, and a control that fires alongside its
treatment reads as confirmation that something real is happening — the
experimenter concludes the effect is robust because two arms moved, when what
happened is that three seeds cannot resolve either.

That is a better argument for the thesis than any of the individual withdrawals,
because it is about the one result that survived. Everything else in this paper
was withdrawn by adding seeds; this shows that the result which *held* would
have been uninterpretable without them, and would have looked fine.

The set of comparisons is taken from the summary files this repository already
wrote, not chosen after seeing which ones make the point. And the honest limit
is in the JSON: the three-seed subset shares its draws with the eight by
construction, so this measures what an experimenter who stopped early would have
concluded, not what a fresh triple would say.

### 97. Correcting entry 96: I picked the tail and called it the distribution

Entry 96's count stands. Its illustration does not.

The count: 48 comparisons at eight seeds, 17 established at p < 0.05, **0
reachable at three** — because the permutation test's floor at three per arm is
0.10 on *every* triple. That is arithmetic and no choice of seeds changes it.

The illustration: I wrote that on `lot`/`cnn_bn`, `Scratch` F1, a three-seed
range screen calls the treatment separated *and its capacity control separated*,
so the experiment "cannot distinguish max pooling helps from a wider head
helps". I called it "the sharpest case" and drew a general conclusion from it.

It came from seeds 0-2, which is one of C(8,3) = 56 ways to pick three.
Enumerating all of them, paired:

| | n | mean % of triples the screen calls separated | never / worst |
|---|---|---|---|
| effects established at eight seeds | 17 | 55% | 0 never |
| comparisons null at eight seeds | 31 | 1% | worst 14% |

**The capacity control fires on 2 of 56 triples, and seeds 0-2 are one of the
two.** I took a 4% event and reported it as what a three-seed experiment would
conclude.

The corrected characterisation is less dramatic and more useful. At three seeds
the range screen has roughly 55% sensitivity to the effects that are real here
and calls a null separated about 1% of the time. That is a defensible screen —
which is exactly what this repository has claimed it is throughout, in the
sentence "a screen, not a verdict". Entry 96 accidentally argued that the screen
is *dangerous*, and the enumeration says it is merely *insensitive*.

**The failure mode is worth naming precisely, because it is not carelessness.**
I had 48 comparisons and picked the one with the most striking pattern to
illustrate a claim I already believed. The pattern was real — those numbers are
correct, that triple does behave that way — and the inference from it was not.
Nothing in the repository's guards could catch this: every number was generated,
nothing was stale, no section vanished. What catches it is asking *how often*
rather than *whether*, which is the same question this project asks of every
effect and which I failed to ask of my own example.

The paper now reports the operating characteristic and says plainly that the
first version picked the tail. The weaker surviving claim — half the established
results here would have been missed by a three-seed protocol, and none could
have been *established* by one — is worth more than the anecdote was, because it
is true of the distribution rather than of one draw.

**Also:** threat 5 was stale within one turn. `add_run_provenance.sh` patched
the runner, so 20 of 666 cells now record `git_sha` and `written_at` — every
cell written since the gap was found, and none written before it. The threat now
says that and states what would retire it: every comparison the paper rests on
re-measured under a recorded commit.

**Postscript to 97: the commit that recorded this correction was itself pushed
with a check failing.** I have been running

    python scripts/check_all.py --quiet 2>&1 | tail -3 && git commit ...

all session. The pipe means `&&` sees `tail`'s exit code, not `check_all`'s, so
the gate has never actually gated anything — every commit this session went
through regardless of what the checks said. It happened to matter only now,
because `WEEKEND.md` was one word over budget when entry 97 was committed.

`check_all.py` was built in entry 79 precisely because reading six separate
outputs is how a failing check got past me, and its whole point is one exit
code. I then piped that exit code into `tail` and read the text instead — the
same failure the tool exists to prevent, reintroduced by how I invoked it. One
word over is a trivial instance; the mechanism is not, and it has been live for
about twenty commits.

The fix is to run the check as its own command and read the verdict line, or
`set -o pipefail`. Recorded here rather than solved by resolution, because a
habit is not a guard: what would actually fix it is a pre-commit hook, and this
repository does not install one because it is a shared environment.

### 98. H74: the failure does not replicate, and the mechanism loses its reach

H74 predicted that `meanmax`'s failure on `size` would replicate on `cnn_bn`,
because the explanation for it — `resize_nearest` couples a defect's apparent
width to native geometry — is a property of the input pipeline, which does not
know which normalisation layer follows. On `Scratch` F1, eight seeds per arm:

| comparison on `size` | difference | exact p |
|---|---|---|
| `cnn_gn`: `meanmax` vs `mean` | -0.0427 | 0.20233 |
| `cnn_bn`: `meanmax` vs `mean` | **+0.0425** | 0.08096 |
| `cnn_bn`: capacity control | +0.0072 | 0.80124 |

**Neither encoder shows an established effect, and the point estimates have
opposite signs.**

I wrote the prediction as a disjunction: "the point estimate is at or below
zero, *or* if positive it does not reach p < 0.05." The second clause is
satisfied, so on a literal reading H74 holds. **Reporting only that would be
dishonest.** The prediction's content was that the failure replicates; a
disjunction broad enough to cover a sign flip is not a prediction, and I should
have noticed when writing it that the second clause made the first unfalsifiable
in practice. That is a lesson about how I phrase hypotheses, not about the data.

Both encoders ran the same eight seeds, so the per-seed difference of
differences is testable exactly. If the mechanism were the whole story it would
be null:

| metric | `cnn_gn` | `cnn_bn` | interaction | seeds | exact p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Scratch` F1 | -0.0427 | +0.0425 | +0.0852 | 7/8 | **0.02344** |
| macro-F1 | -0.0281 | +0.0302 | +0.0583 | 8/8 | **0.00781** |

**It is not null on either metric.** There is an encoder-by-pooling interaction
on geometry holdout that a cause located entirely in the resize cannot produce.

**What survives and what does not.** The model-free measurement stands: the
resize does make a defect's apparent width a function of geometry, geometry
explains 0.7689 of the variance in a max-pooled line-filter response against
0.1485 of the mean-pooled one, and that collapses to 0.0629 at native resolution
under a control that could have killed it. None of that is in question. What is
withdrawn is the *inference* from that measurement to how trained models behave
on `size`. We found a real property of the preprocessing and attached it to a
protocol-level result it does not by itself explain.

So the honest statement about `size` is weaker than the one this project carried
for two days: **the pooling effect is unresolved there on both encoders, its
sign depends on the normalisation layer, and why is unexplained.** The summary
sentence in the paper said "on geometry holdout its mean effect is negative",
which was true of `cnn_gn` and is now encoder-specific; it reads "unresolved on
both encoders, with opposite signs".

The interaction test is post hoc — suggested by the sign disagreement rather
than specified in advance, and one test among many this weekend — so it is
reported as a result that undermines our own explanation rather than as an
established interaction to build on. That asymmetry is deliberate: a post-hoc
finding is weak evidence *for* a new claim and adequate evidence *against* one
we were already making, because it only has to show the old claim's prediction
failed.

**Process:** the `end` index for this edit matched a substring at a shallower
indent, so the replacement left the following block four spaces short and
`paper.py` would not parse. Third time this session; reverting and redoing
against verified line numbers took less time than repairing it. And the commit
gate was checked by exit code this turn rather than by reading a piped tail,
which is how entry 97's postscript said it should have been all along.

### 99. The two surviving results are not independent, and one of them dissolves under the other

Entry 98 found an encoder-by-pooling interaction on `size` and reported it as
specific to geometry holdout. That was too narrow. Checking `lot`, where both
encoders also have eight-seed pooling arms and which needed no new runs:

| metric | protocol | interaction | seeds | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| macro-F1 | `lot` | +0.0106 | 8/8 | **0.00781** |
| macro-F1 | `size` | +0.0583 | 8/8 | **0.00781** |
| `Scratch` | `lot` | -0.0151 | 2/8 | 0.17969 |
| `Scratch` | `size` | +0.0852 | 7/8 | 0.02344 |

On macro-F1 it is present on **both** protocols. So it is not a geometry story,
and entry 98's framing — "an interaction on geometry holdout that a cause
located in the resize cannot produce" — was right that the resize does not
explain it and wrong to tie it to geometry at all.

Asking what the interaction *is* gave a much better answer. `meanmax` closes the
GroupNorm-BatchNorm gap:

| | GN−BN under `mean` | p | GN−BN under `meanmax` | p | gap shrinks | p (change) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `lot` macro-F1 | +0.0162 | **0.0155** | +0.0055 | 0.2151 | 8/8 | **0.00781** |
| `size` macro-F1 | +0.0521 | **0.0163** | -0.0063 | 0.7613 | 8/8 | **0.00781** |
| `size` `Scratch` | +0.0040 | 0.8791 | -0.0812 | **0.0093** | 7/8 | **0.02344** |

**The GroupNorm advantage is established under `mean` on both protocols and
established under `meanmax` on neither.** On `size`/`Scratch` it reverses:
BatchNorm significantly beats GroupNorm once the max is added.

This paper had exactly two surviving positive results, and **one of them is
conditional on the other in a way nothing here noticed.** The GN-vs-BN
comparison was measured with `pool=mean` — that is what the `gnbn` arms carry —
while the pooling result recommends `meanmax`. A reader told "use mean-and-max"
and "use GroupNorm" would reasonably expect the second to hold once they had
done the first. On this corpus it does not.

Neither measurement is wrong. Both were run at eight seeds with exact tests and
both replicate. What was missing is the conditional, and the reason it was
missing is that the two experiments were designed to answer separate questions
and nobody asked whether their answers compose. That is a failure mode this
weekend has not hit before: not an underpowered test, not a stale document, not
a vacuous guard — two correct results whose *conjunction* is false.

**On the strength of the evidence.** The question was raised post hoc, by an
interaction noticed while checking whether the `size` failure replicated, and I
have been careful this weekend about post-hoc comparisons. What makes this more
than an artefact of looking is that it replicates across two protocols
independently — same direction, 8 of 8 seeds each time, p = 0.00781 both times.
And the reported quantity is the *change* in the gap, which is paired by seed
and exact, rather than the `meanmax` comparison alone: "not established" is not
"absent", and the remaining +0.0055 on `lot` is unresolved rather than zero.

The abstract now says the GroupNorm result is conditional on the pooling one,
and section 5.5 carries the measurement.

**Postscript to 99.** Both checks that failed on the first attempt at this entry
were real and both were mine.

The ratchet caught `p = 0.00781` typed into section 5.5 — the sixth time this
session, and again a number I had just read off a terminal while writing prose
about it.

`coverage_check.py` caught something more useful: the four `gn_vs_bn_*` files I
wrote to run the permutation tests were orphans. Section 5.5 reports from
`norm_pooling_interaction.json`, which recomputes the same quantities by a
different route, so nothing read the files the tests had actually produced.

The tempting fix was to delete them, and I created them this session so the
brief allows it. The better one was to check whether the two routes agree —
`gn_vs_bn.py` assembles its arms by globbing run files, `norm_pooling_interaction.py`
by indexing cells — and they do, to the last digit on all four comparisons. That
is now a line in the paper, which makes the files non-orphans and records a
verification that would otherwise have been thrown away. Most of this weekend's
errors were in the plumbing rather than the statistics: a glob matching zero
files, a seed missing from a key, an arm spec parsed as an encoder name. Two
independent routes to the same p-value is cheap evidence against exactly that
class of error, and I had it sitting on disk without looking at it.
